text:
No directly matching controlled study surfaced that isolates a terminal-MASK loss coefficient while holding terminal-example frequency and prefix-context distribution fixed. Original [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690) already includes last-item-only masked training examples, so terminal supervision itself is established. Its one-mask versus multi-mask comparison reports HR@10 rising from 0.2940 to 0.3025 on Beauty and 0.6869 to 0.6970 on ML-1m. This supports richer Cloze supervision, but does not isolate terminal weighting: target counts and available context change together.

Related evidence reinforces the confounding concern. [Recency Sampling](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643) changes target selection and conditioning histories, reporting up to 16% higher NDCG than fully trained BERT4Rec with 93% less training time using RSS-enhanced SASRec; this is not evidence for a terminal coefficient within BERT4Rec. In language modeling, [Wettig et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2202.08005) explicitly separate corruption rate from prediction rate: more prediction signals aid optimization, whereas more corruption makes reconstruction harder. Their 40%-masking model improves SQuAD F1 from 88.0 to 89.8 despite perplexity worsening from 17.7 to 69.4—an analogous reconstruction/downstream tradeoff, not recommendation evidence.

Implication for the proposed experiment: explicit weighting is a plausible controlled hypothesis, not a demonstrated ranking improvement or established novelty claim. Use one BERT4Rec network with separately normalized losses, L = L_MLM + λL_terminal; vary λ on identical sampled prefixes, terminal examples, corruption masks, and update budgets. Separately vary terminal-example allocation at fixed λ, then prefix sampling. Measure pinned validation HR@10 alongside fixed-probe interior reconstruction and terminal cross-entropy to reveal any tradeoff.
